Source slide page 1 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY (UE26CY151 A,B)

Department of Science and Humanities

Source slide page 2 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Class 31 content: 
Fuel Cells: Principle, working & H2-O2 fuel cell

Source slide page 3 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Fuel cells

Chemical energy   Thermal energy  Mechanical energy  Electrical energy 	
                                                Fuel cell
Galvanic cell which converts chemical energy of a fuel oxidant system directly into electrical energy by means of redox reactions
Do not store energy but convert chemical energy in the fuel to electrical energy
Fuel and oxidising agents have to be continuously supplied at the respective electrodes
Generate power as long as the electroactive material is supplied

Source slide page 4 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Working:

Anode : Fuel   Oxidation product + ne-
Cathode : Oxidant + ne-   Reduction products



Fuels : H2, CO, CH3OH, C2H5OH, HCHO, N2H4
Oxidants: O2 , H2O2, halogens

Source slide page 5 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Advantages :
 High power efficiency (about 50 - 80% )
 Ecofriendly -  products formed are not toxic
 Silent operation
Disadvantages : 
 Cost of the power is high as a result of the use of  
        expensive electrodes and catalysts
 Power out put is moderate
 Fuels in the form of gases and oxygen need to be stored in
        tanks under high pressure-special equipment is required

Source slide page 6 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Applications:

  Space exploration; as auxiliary power generators in space
       vehicles
   Vehicle traction for cars, buses and commercial vehicles
   Large scale power generation

Source slide page 7 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Alkaline fuel cell - H2 – O2 alkaline fuel cell
  Aqueous solution of KOH is used as electrolyte
  Low temperature fuel cell (operates at 100oC) 
  Oxygen reduction is more rapid in alkaline electrolytes 
         than in acid electrolytes
  Use of non noble metal electro-catalyst is feasible
  Carbon containing fuels cannot be used as CO2 is
        formed as product which reacts with the electrolyte, KOH, to form K2CO3 which reduces efficiency of the cell
                  CO2 + KOH  K2CO3 + H2O

Source slide page 8 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Construction : 

Anode : Porous carbon with Pt catalyst
Cathode : Porous carbon with Ag catalyst
Fuel : Hydrogen gas      
 Oxidant : Oxygen gas
Electrolyte : 30-45 % KOH(warm)

Source slide page 10 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Working:

H2 gas diffuses through anode ,gets adsorbed on the electrode surface ,reacts with OH- to form water
 At cathode O2 diffuses through electrode, is adsorbed and reduced to OH-
 Product is water which dilutes the KOH
 Cell operates at 100oC, so that water from KOH escapes as steam
The water was used by astronauts for drinking on Apollo spacecraft

 Emf = 1.23 V

Source slide page 11 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Advantages: 
Operates at low temperature
Alkali is used as electrolyte hence non noble metal catalyst  can
        be used so less expensive

Disadvantages:

Reactants must be free from C, because on oxidation CO2 is formed .The alkali reacts with CO2 to form carbonates which reduce efficiency of the cells; pure fuel and oxidant which are free of carbon compounds must be used
Liquid electrolytes pose handling problems

Transcript block 1 (source interval 000000-000299 seconds):
[00:00:00.484] Hello everyone, welcome back to this course on engineering chemistry. We will continue with module 5 on energy storage devices on fuel cells. So today we are going to learn about fuel cells principle and working advantages, disadvantages and applications.
[00:00:19.908] So, what are fuel cells? In a thermal power plant, we know that combus of fuel is done and power is generated from there. But this happens in several steps. So when combustion of fuel takes place, the chemical energy is stored inside the fuel.
[00:00:39.152] When the fuel burns, there is heat generated. So we converted chemical energy into thermal energy. This thermal energy is used to run turbines. So we have converted now again thermal energy to mechanical energy. These turbines now are used to generate power. So mechanical energy got converted.
[00:00:58.352] To electrical energy, but at each step there is a loss of efficiency. So finally, the efficiency is just 35 to 40 percent.
[00:01:09.892] The idea in a fuel cell is can we convert the chemical energy directly into the electrical energy? If that is done.
[00:01:20.208] We will definitely have a better efficiency, and that is exactly what is done in a fuel cell. The chemical energy is directly converted into electrical energy, and we find that the efficiency is about 75 to 80 percent. So how is this done?
[00:01:38.948] The combustion of fuel, that is, say for example, hydrogen and oxygen. Hydrogen is the fuel and oxygen is the oxidant is done in the form of galvanic cell.
[00:01:52.592] Now we know that when we want to make a galvanic cell, then we need a redox reaction. So what is the redox reaction? Let us check whether the combustion of fuel is a redox reaction. So let's say we have hydrogen plus oxygen is giving you water.
[00:02:12.132] So we know that when hydrogen undergoes combustion in oxygen, we get water. So is this a redox reaction?
[00:02:20.528] We can see very clear hydrogen is getting oxidized to water and oxygen is getting reduced to water. So therefore, we know that combustion of a fuel it is a redox reaction. And we know in a galvanic cell we can use this redox reaction.
[00:02:39.168] How we can make the reaction happen in two different compartments, meaning that we will not allow the hydrogen and oxygen to uh come in contact, but we will allow the hydrogen to undergo oxidation at the anode and oxygen to undergo reduction at the cathode. Now
[00:02:56.816] Since hydrogen is undergoing oxidation
[00:03:00.048] At the anode electrons will be generated and these electrons are going to move through the external wire towards the cathode where there is oxygen and that is going to absorb the electrons and undergo reduction. So basically we have allowed
[00:03:16.912] the combustion reaction to happen in two separate compartments at anode and cathode and thereby we are generating electrical power. So the chemical energy in the reaction has been converted directly into the redox reaction. So this is the concept of a fuel cell.
[00:03:36.388] So whatever is the chemical energy of the fuel oxygen system is getting directly converted into electrical energy by means of a redox reaction. So we can understand that here, what is the difference between a regular battery and a fuel cell?
[00:03:53.200] Now in a regular battery we know that the reactants, the electroactive material are stored inside the battery.
[00:04:01.376] And they are they undergo reaction, and that is how we get power from the battery. But a fuel cell, though it is also a galvanic cell, is different from a battery. Why? Because the fuel and the oxidant, that is the electroactive material, have to be supplied.
[00:04:19.024] Continuously from outside as at the respective electrodes. So meaning that we do not store energy inside the battery, but the chemical energy of the fuel is converted into electrical energy.
[00:04:36.720] So we can say that though batteries are energy storage devices, whereas fuel cells are energy conversion devices. So in a
[00:04:50.084] Fuel cell, the fuel and the oxidizing agents have to be continuously supplied. They will be able to generate power only as long as the electroactive material is supplied at the anode and the cathode.

Now let us write the cell representation. So what do we see? We always start with the anode, like in any galvanic cell.

[00:11:07.024] uh oxidizing agents so it can be used and then halogens we know are good oxidizing agents. So these are the fuels and the oxidants that can be used in a fuel cell.
[00:11:20.036] Now, what are the advantages of the fuel cell? Of course, we understand the efficiency is very high, much higher than what we see in the uh thermal power station.
[00:11:33.828] The efficiency is about 50 to 80 percent in the case of a fuel cell, and most importantly, they are eco-friendly because the products which are formed are not toxic. So in the case, suppose we have hydrogen and oxygen, we get
[00:11:51.072] uh water in the if we are using any carbon monoxide we get carbon dioxide. If we are using methanol we are going to get carbon dioxide and water. So they are all uh eco-friendly products which are getting formed unlike when uh this uh
[00:12:06.532] They undergo combustion, the which are used in uh vehicles, we know that there's a lot of pollution happening due to the
[00:12:14.980] Products being given out into the uh atmosphere. And then another thing, another important fact is that the advantage is that it they have a very silent operation. Unlike in a thermal power plant, there is there is a there is no noise when such a
[00:12:32.144] uh power generation is happening in the fuel cell. But there are certain disadvantages also. The cost of power is very high. Why? Because we have to go for expensive
[00:12:44.144] uh electrodes and also catalysts. More uh important are the catalysts because they have to be present for the reaction to take place. And these catalysts, electrocatalysts especially, are expensive.
[00:12:57.760] So and also the power output is moderate in this case. And one more important fact is that fuels which are used in the form of uh gases.
[00:13:10.468] and oxygen they have to be stored in tanks under high pressure. So special equipment is required. Hydrogen is a very good fuel, but storing hydrogen is the biggest challenge
[00:13:26.720] for using the fuel cells. So these are certain disadvantages which are there for the fuel cells.
[00:13:37.156] What are the applications? Yes, space exploration. All of us are aware that it started a long time back and NASA uses these fuel cells right from the Apollo space program. So they are very useful for.
[00:13:53.956] powering the space vehicles. So they are an auxiliary power. They act as auxiliary power generators in space vehicles and also vehicle traction.
[00:14:06.340] for cars, buses and commercial vehicles, they are looked upon as the next generation uh power uh generators for cars, buses and commercial vehicles.
[00:14:18.768] So vehicle traction, traction means moving, when when you're you using not fuel, but you're using the battery or the galvanic cell is being used, in this case the fuel cell is being used to power the motor to run the machine.
[00:14:34.560] So and then of course large scale power generation if that would be possible. Stationary applications uh have been uh done to a great extent, but still mobile applications are still being researched. So if that comes then
[00:14:53.220] we are going to be uh very well placed as far as power powering the vehicles is uh concerned because we know that the non-renewable resources like petroleum, etcetera, the fossil fuels.

Transcript block 4 (source interval 000900-001199 seconds):
[00:15:09.136] They are depleting fast, so if we could get these fuel cells to power the cars, buses and commercial vehicles and also for large scale power generation, it is going to be very useful in future.
[00:15:25.552] Let us do efficiency of a fuel cell. So efficiency of a fuel cell as any efficiency of a machine is thermodynamic efficiency, which is given by ratio of the work output to the heat input.
[00:15:42.704] Any efficiency is always measured by what is the output work done by the input, uh input heat in this case. So what is the work output in the case of a fuel cell?
[00:15:55.024] We can say it is the electrical energy which we are electrical work which are which we are getting from the fuel cell, and that is given by the Gibbs free energy.
[00:16:06.948] Gives free energy because we know that delta G is equal to minus N FE.
[00:16:16.484] So we know that the electrical output which you get, the the electrical energy which we get from the battery is because of the Gibbs free energy. So if we know the Gibbs free energy, we know what is the work output. And what is the heat input in this case? It is the enthalpy change which happens.
[00:16:34.176] During the cell reaction. Which reaction are we talking about? We are talking about the combustion of the fuel. So whenever the fuel burns in oxygen or any other oxidant, then the heat which is released is the is the
[00:16:50.016] uh heat input that is because the chemical energy is what we are inputting in in uh using as input in the uh fuel cell. So therefore we have
[00:16:59.780] Heat input is enthalpy change of the cell reaction and the work output is the Gibbs free energy. So Gibbs free energy delta G as I mentioned just now is a measure of the electrical work done, and enthalpy change delta H is the measure of the heat released during the reaction. So when we calculate
[00:17:17.552] The efficiency is given in the form of percentage. That would be it's denoted by the symbol, this uh this symbol percentage that is delta G by delta H. That is the
[00:17:29.520] uh work output by the heat input multiplied by 100 and since delta g is given by minus nf e we can write this as minus nf e by delta h into 100. So this is how we calculate the efficiency of a fuel cell.
